about: "Make it specific" prompts for unit-7 (docs/aphug-architecture.md, "Make it specific"); checked by checkJustify in scripts/lib/aphug-exams.mjs.

prompts.title: Describing an industrial city
prompts.prompt: Describe Manchester, England, as an industrial city of the early 1800s.
checklist: Names the industry and its power source
Says how the city grew and who moved there
Describes conditions, more than a label

earns.answer: In the early 1800s, Manchester, England, filled with steam-powered cotton mills; workers moved in from farms, the city grew fast, and its crowded housing and smoky air made it a symbol of the new industrial city.
earns.why: It names the industry, growth and conditions.

misses.answer: Manchester was an industrial city in England.
misses.why: A label with nothing about what the city was like.

why.1: Cars came about a century later.

prompts.title: From steel to services in Pittsburgh
prompts.prompt: Explain why Pittsburgh's economy shifted from steel to health care and education after the 1980s.
checklist: Names why the steel mills closed
Links that to the loss of secondary jobs
Says which sectors replaced them

earns.answer: Many of Pittsburgh's steel mills closed in the 1980s as cheaper steel came from abroad and from newer mills, so the city lost much of its secondary sector, and hospitals and universities, such as the University of Pittsburgh's medical center, became its largest employers.
earns.why: It names the cause, the loss and the replacement, linked.

misses.answer: Pittsburgh used to make steel and now has hospitals.
misses.why: It states the before and after but never says why it changed.

cause.label: Why mills closed
options: cheaper steel from abroad and newer mills
the city ran out of rivers

why.1: Coal is primary, not the growth sector.

prompts.title: GNI per capita and HDI
prompts.prompt: Compare GNI per capita and the Human Development Index as measures of development.
checklist: Says what each measure counts
Says how the two measures differ
Says what that difference allows: similar income, different HDI

earns.answer: GNI per capita measures only income per person, whereas the HDI combines income with health (life expectancy) and education (years of schooling), so two countries with similar incomes can have quite different HDI values.
earns.why: It names what each measures and what the difference means.

misses.answer: The HDI is a better measure of development than GNI.
misses.why: A verdict without saying what either one measures.

sideA.label: GNI per capita
options: the size of the economy alone

why.1: Those are parts of the HDI.
The HDI adds health and education.
why.2: Population is not part of the HDI.

prompts.title: Do microloans raise women's incomes?
prompts.prompt: Explain the degree to which microloans raise women's incomes.
checklist: States the degree first: to a limited degree, for example
Names a real program with its date
Uses research results on both sides

earns.answer: To a limited degree: Bangladesh's Grameen Bank, founded in 1983, lent small sums mostly to women to start businesses, and many repaid and earned income, but studies of microloans in several countries found only modest average gains in income, so they help some women without lifting most out of poverty.
earns.why: It states the degree and backs it with a program and evidence on both sides.

misses.answer: Microloans help women start businesses in Bangladesh.
misses.why: No degree stated, and only one side of the evidence.

why.1: Studies found modest gains, not complete change.

prompts.title: Naming a place: a special economic zone
prompts.context: A student writes: "Some countries made zones to attract foreign factories."
prompts.prompt: Rewrite the claim with a real place, its year and what happened.
checklist: Names a real zone and its year
Says what the zone offered
Gives the result for the place

earns.answer: Shenzhen, China, became a special economic zone in 1980, with low taxes and fewer rules for foreign firms, and it grew from a small town into a city of millions making electronics for export.
earns.why: It names the place, year, terms and result.

misses.answer: China made special zones for factories to attract companies.
misses.why: No named zone, no year and no result, so a reader cannot check it.

kind.label: What it offered
options: low taxes and fewer rules for foreign firms

why.1: Zones lower costs to attract firms.
why.2: The point was to attract foreign firms.

prompts.title: Ecotourism at two scales
prompts.prompt: Explain how ecotourism in Costa Rica connects the global and local scales.
checklist: Names the global scale: tourists from many countries
Names the local scale: a named village or park
Explains the link: income from protecting forest

earns.answer: At the global scale, tourists from many countries travel to Costa Rica to see its rainforests, and at the local scale, towns near parks such as Monteverde earn income from guiding and lodging, so protecting the forest pays locally.
earns.why: It names both scales with places and links them.

misses.answer: Tourists visit Costa Rica's rainforests every year to see wildlife.
misses.why: It names no scale of analysis and no local place that gains.

why.2: A city is not the global scale.

prompts.title: How well Rostow fits
prompts.prompt: Explain how well Rostow's stages of economic growth fit South Korea, and give one limit of the model.
checklist: Names the stage South Korea's growth is often read as
Says why South Korea's growth fits that stage
Gives a limit of the model

earns.answer: Rostow's model fits South Korea fairly well, because its fast growth in factory exports from the 1960s is often read as a take-off; but the model assumes every country can follow Britain's path on its own, so it ignores how colonial ties and the world economy shape a country's chances.
earns.why: It applies the model to a named case with a date, and gives a limit.

misses.answer: Rostow's model says countries go through five stages.
misses.why: A description of the model, not how it fits a case or where it fails.

why.1: South Korea industrialized fast from the 1960s.

limit.label: Limit
options: it assumes one path for all countries

why.1: The number of stages is not the main criticism.
why.2: That is the demographic transition model.

prompts.title: What GDP misses
prompts.prompt: Explain one limitation of GDP as a measure of development, using a named city.
checklist: Names what GDP leaves out: informal and unpaid work
Gives a real city as an example
Says which way GDP is off

earns.answer: GDP counts only recorded market activity, so the informal work of street vendors in cities such as Lagos, Nigeria, and unpaid work at home are left out, and the figure can understate how much a country produces.
earns.why: It names the gap, a city and the direction of the error.

misses.answer: GDP does not measure how happy people are in a country.
misses.why: True but not about what GDP counts; the point is the work it misses.

prompts.title: Reading an income-group map legend
prompts.context: A world map shades countries by World Bank FY27 income group (July 2026 to June 2027), based on 2025 GNI per person (Atlas method): low (up to $1,175), lower-middle ($1,176 to $4,635), upper-middle ($4,636 to $14,375) and high (over $14,375).
prompts.prompt: Explain what a country's shade tells you, and what it does not.
checklist: Reads a class with its range and year
Says what the shade measures: average income
Says what it leaves out: how income is shared, health, schooling

earns.answer: A country shaded upper-middle income had a 2025 GNI per person between $4,636 and $14,375, the World Bank's FY27 thresholds, so it sits in that band of average income; the shade says nothing about how income is shared or about health and schooling.
earns.why: It reads a class with its range and year, and names what the shade leaves out.

misses.answer: Dark countries are rich and light countries are poor.
misses.why: It reads no class or year and says nothing of what the shade leaves out.

limit.label: What it leaves out
options: how income is shared, health and schooling

why.1: Average income is what it shows.

prompts.title: Why service work moved to Bengaluru
prompts.prompt: Explain why many companies outsourced customer service and software work to Bengaluru, India, from the 1990s.
checklist: Names at least two reasons: English speakers and lower wages
Names the technology that cut the cost of distance
Links the reasons to the companies' decision

earns.answer: Many people in India speak English and wages there were lower than in the United States, and fast internet and phone links cut the cost of distance, so companies could move customer service and software work to cities such as Bengaluru and save money.
earns.why: It names the reasons and links them to the decision.

misses.answer: Bengaluru has a lot of technology companies and call centers.
misses.why: It states a fact but never explains why the work moved there.

why.2: Fast internet links made it possible.

link.label: Link
options: so wages rose in the United States

why.2: The work moved; it did not stop.
